articles.summary: Thermal Dynamics, an ESAB brand, unveiled its next generation of manual plasma cutters, Cutmaster 90X and Cutmaster 110X, in booth #S29025 at FABTECH 2026 in Las Vegas. The Cutmaster X series features a consumables design and patented arc starting mechanism that has no moving parts.
articles.body: Thermal Dynamics Launches New Cutmaster 90X and 110X Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Credit: Thermal Dynamics Thermal Dynamics, an ESAB brand, unveiled its next generation of manual plasma cutters, Cutmaster 90X and Cutmaster 110X, in booth #S29025 at FABTECH 2026 in Las Vegas. The Cutmaster X series features a consumables design and patented arc starting mechanism that has no moving parts. After establishing airflow, it starts the arc in a few thousandths of a second, improving cutting performance. The Cutmaster X series also features the patented 1Torch X, which has an articulating head that can flex 30 to 90 degrees, then lock in place, to improve joint access for cutting and gouging. The Cutmaster X series enables location flexibility for the shop and field. It automatically connects to 200 – 600V, 1ph and 3ph primary power without manual linking and provides a steady arc even if primary voltage varies.The Cutmaster 90X has a rated pierce and cut capacity of 7/8 in. and a 1.75 in. sever capability. The Cutmaster 110X has a rated pierce and cut capacity of 1 in. and a 2 in. sever capability. At nameplate output, they have a 50% duty cycle using 208V, 1ph primary power, and duty cycle increases at higher power inputs. Both units weigh approximately 87 lbs. The machine ships with a cutting tip, gouging tip, two cups, and five caps for cutting. The 1Torch X has cable length options of 20, 40, 60, 80 or 100 ft. A new industrial housing protects the unit in rugged environments, and a large, digital display, intuitive menus and choice of 29 different languages makes operation and training easy. Other features include automatic inlet/outlet air pressure detection, automatic post-cut air purge to extend consumables life and a 14-pin CPC connection for semi-automated applications. Target markets include heavy industrial and general fabrication, manufacturing, construction, repair/maintenance, pipelines, foundries, railcars, marine, offshore and training schools.

articles.title: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan
articles.summary: China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines.Responding…
articles.body: China Militia Boats Expand 'Battlefield Prep', says Taiwan Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Copyright TomKorcak/AdobeStock China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand "battlefield preparation" around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, Taiwan's Coast Guard said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines. Responding to a Reuters exclusive this month on the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat off Taiwan's Pacific coast in mid-August, the coast guard said it had dispatched a patrol boat to drive away the vessel, which was operating alongside a Chinese coast guard ship and a research vessel. The coast guard confirmed details in the Reuters report, identifying the suspected militia fishing boat as Minfudingyu 07902 , and said it had come as close as about 2.7 nautical miles outside Taiwan's restricted waters on August 16. China has increased such activity since June in overlapping economic waters involving Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, the coast guard said, after Tokyo and Manila announced talks on maritime boundary delimitation in their exclusive economic zones. EEZs extend 200 nautical miles from the coast and give a coastal state rights to exploit, conserve and manage natural resources in those waters. "Such complex grey-zone operations not only increase the maritime surveillance and response burden on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, but may also create regional security pressure and affect the existing international maritime order," Taiwan's Coast Guard said in a statement to Reuters. China's defence ministry, and the Philippines defence and foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Japan's coast guard declined immediate comment. The coast guard said the vessels' coordinated activity was part of a broader pattern of Chinese "grey-zone" operations using law-enforcement, scientific and civilian cover to expand Beijing's influence at sea while remaining below the threshold of open conflict. The Chinese operations were aimed at "assisting 'battlefield preparation'," the coast guard said, adding Taiwan's east coast was an important maritime traffic and supply route and that continued Chinese activity there could further increase security pressure on Taiwan. Officials in Taiwan say they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve its goals. Taiwan's government rejects the claim and says only the island's people can decide their future. China has repeatedly said its operations off Taiwan's east coast are "legitimate and lawful" because they are in Chinese waters, a position Taipei's government strongly rejects. Taiwan's coast guard said it had placed the Minfudingyu 07902 on a priority watchlist, assessing the boat showed the "characteristics" of Chinese maritime militia activity and said it would continue tracking the vessel. Dating back to the 1950s, China's maritime militia uses fishing vessels with trained, state-supported crews to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships around South China Sea flashpoints, helping Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance. The surveillance report reviewed by Reuters was conducted by Taiwan's Apex Aviation, which used radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data from a reconnaissance flight to document the cluster of vessels. (Reuters)

articles.summary: The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing...

REUTERS/Carlos Barria/File Photo The Trump administration is proposing to extend its suspension of port fees targeting China-linked vessels for another two months, pushing their potential return into January 2027 as Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. The proposal, outlined in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication October 26, would extend the existing one-year suspension through January 9, 2027. The current pause is set to expire November 9. The extension would provide another reprieve for shipping companies facing potentially significant fees on Chinese-owned, Chinese-operated and Chinese-built vessels calling at U.S. ports, as well as certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. “The United States is continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices at issue in the investigation,” USTR said in the notice. Under the proposal, the measures would remain suspended from November 10, 2026, through January 9, 2027. During that period, shipping companies would not incur liability for port fees under Annexes I, II and III of the original Section 301 action. The suspension would also continue to cover certain duties on ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment. The proposed extension comes nearly a year after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to suspend the port fees as part of a broader trade agreement reached in South Korea. Washington began collecting the fees on October 14, 2025, but suspended them on November 10, meaning the measures were in effect for less than four weeks. China also suspended its retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. The original measures emerged from a Section 301 investigation launched during the Biden administration following a 2024 petition by the United Steelworkers and other labor organizations. The investigation concluded that China’s industrial policies and subsidies distorted global competition and undermined U.S. commerce. The resulting port fees became a central part of the Trump administration’s strategy to counter China’s maritime dominance and encourage investment in American shipbuilding. Growing Pressure to Reinstate Fees The latest proposal comes despite mounting pressure from some lawmakers and maritime labor groups to bring the fees back. In June, Senators Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) urged the administration to immediately reinstate the measures , arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild the U.S. commercial shipbuilding industry. “Section 301 port fees are critical to revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding,” the senators wrote in a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The lawmakers pointed to China’s growing share of global shipbuilding, noting that Chinese yards now account for more than half of global commercial vessel production, compared with just 0.1% for the United States. They also questioned whether Washington had secured meaningful concessions from Beijing in exchange for suspending the fees and how the administration intended to fund its proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund without the revenue. Maritime labor unions have similarly criticized the suspension, arguing that it weakens one of the few measures specifically designed to counter China’s state-supported shipbuilding industry. Shipping companies, meanwhile, have welcomed the reprieve. The original fees threatened to impose substantial costs on carriers and disrupt established shipping networks. During the brief period the measures were active, U.S. carrier Matson reported incurring $6.4 million in reciprocal Chinese port fees, while China’s state-owned COSCO faced an estimated $1.5 billion in annual U.S. charges. Andy Abbott, CEO of ACL, told gCaptain that any port fees would impact its growing US export business, and customers are concerned ACL. “ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” explained Abbott. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade. This development allows us to continue serving the US market with the fastest transit times from the US East Coast to Europe.” The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) and World Shipping Council both welcomed last year’s suspension, warning that the competing U.S. and Chinese measures risked increasing transportation costs and disrupting global trade. A Broader Debate Over Port Fees The proposed extension also comes as the administration considers a much broader port fee system under its Maritime Action Plan , unveiled earlier this year. Unlike the China-specific Section 301 measures, the plan envisions fees on all foreign-built commercial vessels calling at U.S. ports, with proceeds supporting domestic shipbuilding through a proposed Maritime Security Trust Fund. The plan outlined potential fees ranging from 1 cent to 25 cents per kilogram of imported cargo, which the administration estimated could generate as much as $1.5 trillion over 10 years at the upper end. ICS has warned that such broad-based charges could significantly increase shipping costs and disrupt global trade, even as it supports efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity. The proposals underscore the competing pressures facing the administration as it seeks to revive American shipyards without imposing additional costs on U.S. importers, exporters and consumers. For now, the latest USTR proposal would leave the China-specific port fee measures on hold for another two months, while negotiations continue. USTR has opened a public comment period on the extension, with submissions due by 5 p.m. Eastern Time on October 30. Comments can be filed through the USTR public comment portal under docket USTR-2026-0694. The extension has not yet been finalized. The notice also does not address whether China will extend its own suspension of retaliatory fees on U.S.-linked vessels. articles.title: Record Tanker Rates Threaten to Push U.S. Oil Exports to Asia to Seven-Year Low
articles.summary: US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Yongchang Chin and Nathan Risser (Bloomberg) –US crude oil exports to Asia are set to hit multi-year lows after the Iran war disrupted global shipping and pushed the cost to lease a tanker for the Pacific journey to a record of almost $80 million. Asian refinery orders for US crude for delivery in November tumbled roughly 50% to 24 million to 26 million barrels this month sequentially, according to traders who asked for anonymity because they weren’t authorized to publicly comment. If that pace of orders holds through the end of this month, it would mark a seven-year low, based on ship-tracking data from Kpler and Vortexa. The tanker rate along the US Gulf Coast-to-China route has more than tripled since the US-Iran conflict erupted in late February to almost $60 million as of Thursday, according to Baltic Exchange figures. Earlier in the month, it touched $79.6 million, an unprecedented ruction in a market where rates averaged less than $8 million in the half decade before the conflict. As it stands, leasing the largest class of crude carriers for the 30-day voyage is equivalent to half the cost of building a brand-new vessel. Those eye-watering rates doesn’t include the cost of the oil itself, which is trading around $100 a barrel. Cost to Ship US Oil to Asia Has Never Been Higher “The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, Valero Energy Inc.’s head of oil trading, said during as conference call with analysts. Tanker rates are so inflated that refiners are effectively spending $30 to $35 to haul each barrel of crude from the Gulf Coast to Asia, or as much as seven times what they shelled out last year, Hawkins said. IEA: Gulf Oil Shipping Costs Top $37 Per Barrel, Five Times Pre-War Levels To be sure, the end of the November trading cycle isn’t a hard deadline, which leaves some leeway for traders to snap up last-minutes cargoes. At least one market participant who asked to remain anonymous said Asia-bound US cargoes for November may recover to as much as 40 million barrels in post-cycle trades. Vortexa, however, is skeptical that such a turnaround is imminent. “We don’t currently see evidence of a near-term surge that would push those volumes significantly higher,” said Rohit Rathod, a senior Vortexa analyst. The drop in Asian demand appears to be rippling across US crude pricing. Export-bound Permian Basin oil was trading for 25 cents above the benchmark futures contract at the Magellan East Houston hub as of Wednesday, down from more than $3 six weeks earlier, according to Link Data Services. Medium sour export grade Mars, which is pumped from deepwater wells in the Gulf of Mexico and is similar to Middle Eastern crude, has seen its premium to futures plunge to $6 from $17.50 in late March. US Oil Exports Surged to Record High This Year | The US sent over 6 million barrels of oil abroad each day in late April as war curtailed flows from the Middle East Valero’s Hawkins said one factor hindering global tanker availability has been the increased use of smaller vessels to pick up crude in the Persian Gulf that are less likely to be hit by Iranian fire in Strait of Hormuz. Once they’ve traversed the waterway, their cargoes are transferred to larger vessels waiting in the Gulf of Oman. “The inefficient process of this ship-to-ship transferring that they’re doing of crude oil in the Gulf of Oman is really tying up global shipping and to require more tankers to move the same amount of oil,” Hawkins said. Insurance rates and high fuel costs also are driving up freight costs, he added. “The primary factor remains high freight costs, which continue to squeeze arbitrage economics for long-haul routes,” Vortexa’s Rathod said. “The incentive for Asian buyers to source from the US Gulf Coast has diminished.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.summary: A tanker carrying Russian diesel is expected to arrive in Norfolk, Virginia, on November 2, potentially becoming the first such shipment to reach the United States in more than three...

A tanker carrying Russian diesel is expected to arrive in Norfolk, Virginia, on November 2, potentially becoming the first such shipment to reach the United States in more than three years. The Vietnamese-flagged PVT Azura (IMO 9423683), reportedly carrying 109,000 barrels of Russian diesel, departed St. Petersburg on October 15 and is currently signaling Norfolk as its destination, according to VesselFinder . The arrival would come five days ahead of another Russian diesel shipment identified by Reuters on Friday as the first cargo heading to the United States under a recent agreement between President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low-sulfur diesel, equivalent to approximately 300,000 barrels, at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22. The tanker has signaled New York as its destination, with an expected arrival date of November 7, although its final discharge port has not been confirmed. The two shipments come as the Trump administration moves to ease restrictions on Russian diesel in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. On October 9, Trump announced an agreement under which Russia would immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter. The same day, the U.S. Treasury Department issued General License 135 , authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027. On October 16, one day after the PVT Azura departed St. Petersburg, Trump also signed an executive order waiving sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act. Trump said the waiver was “in the national interests of the United States.” The shipments would mark a rare return of Russian diesel to American ports following the Biden administration’s 2022 ban on Russian energy imports. According to the Associated Press, the last delivery of Russian diesel to the United States occurred in July 2023. The PVT Azura is a conventional product tanker owned by PetroVietnam Transportation Corporation, according to classification records, with a history of transporting Russian petroleum products. According to MyShipTracking.com, the vessel has called at several ports this year, including St. Petersburg and Svetly in Russia, the José Terminal in Venezuela, Constan?a in Romania, Szczecin in Poland, and Botlek, a major petroleum storage hub in the Port of Rotterdam, Netherlands. On February 15, the PVT Azura suffered engine failure and went adrift in Germany’s Kiel Canal. Two tugs responded and towed the tanker back toward Kiel, but sanctions related to Russian oil shipments reportedly prevented it from berthing at a German port. The tanker is reportedly not headed to the Port of Virginia’s commercial terminals in Norfolk, but instead to a facility associated with U.S. military operations. The precise discharge location and intended use of the cargo have not been independently confirmed. The U.S. Coast Guard did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication. “This effort shows other players in the oil industry that the U.S. is open for business when it comes to buying Russian diesel,” said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. The arrival of the PVT Azura would provide an early test of the administration’s decision to reopen the U.S. market to Russian diesel, even as questions remain over how much additional supply Moscow can deliver and whether the shipments will meaningfully reduce fuel prices. The overall index declined by 74 points, or 2.6%, bringing it back towards more typical levels after its record-setting performance. All sector indices ended the week lower. DLSI Owners recorded the steepest decline, losing 263 points, equivalent to a contraction of 6.7%. DLSI Carriers also posted a triple-digit points loss and fell by 2.6%. Negative sentiment was widespread, with 83 companies recording share-price declines and only 35 finishing the week higher. The average movement represented a decrease of more than 2% per company. Among the limited number of gainers, New Zealand-based Move Logistics led the advance with a 9% increase, while major container carrier HMM gained 6%. Nine companies recorded declines of at least 10%. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.80, or 1.8%, to $101.27. The Brent benchmark is on track for a 4.4% weekly rise, its third in a row, while WTI is poised to finish 0.4% down on the week. Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered the evacuation of its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reported, as fighting intensified between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen-based Houthis. An oil spill from a tanker was detected off the UAE coast of Umm Al Quwain, the United Arab Emirates Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Friday. Clashes between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition that backs Yemen's internationally recognised government have raged since the Iran-aligned Houthis pushed towards Bab el-Mandeb last month, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea. In Libya, an oil pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara oilfields to Zawiya port has been shut, leading to a reduction in production at both fields, the head of the National Oil Corporation told Reuters on Thursday. articles.summary: South Korea’s push to help rebuild the American shipbuilding industry is moving beyond investments in existing shipyards and toward the development of entirely new production capacity. The latest example comes...

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries/Handout via REUTERS/File Photo South Korea’s push to help rebuild the American shipbuilding industry is moving beyond investments in existing shipyards and toward the development of entirely new production capacity. The latest example comes from HD Hyundai, one of the world’s largest shipbuilders, which has announced plans to develop a new U.S. shipyard in partnership with American engineering and construction giant Kiewit. The proposed joint venture, HD Kiewit Shipbuilding, would combine South Korean shipbuilding technology with American engineering, fabrication and construction expertise. The companies are targeting construction beginning in 2027, with full-scale operations by 2029 and the potential to create up to 3,000 jobs. But the significance extends beyond another planned shipyard. The project represents a potentially important step in South Korea’s $150 billion commitment to rebuilding U.S. shipbuilding capacity under the Make American Shipbuilding Great Again, or MASGA, initiative. It also highlights two different approaches emerging among South Korea’s shipbuilding giants: Hanwha is investing heavily in expanding an existing American shipyard, while HD Hyundai is pursuing an entirely new production facility built around modern manufacturing technology. HD Hyundai and Kiewit first announced a strategic partnership in July, laying the groundwork for cooperation on U.S. shipbuilding projects, including the fabrication of ship blocks and modules. The latest agreement takes that relationship considerably further. Rather than simply supplying technology or helping modernize existing facilities, the companies envision a purpose-built shipyard on an existing industrial site with deepwater access to the Gulf of Mexico. Although the companies have not formally identified the location, Kiewit already operates a major offshore fabrication complex in Ingleside, Texas, near Corpus Christi, where it has spent decades constructing large offshore energy structures. The facility has the waterfront access, heavy industrial fabrication experience and infrastructure needed for major marine construction projects. Kiewit has previously fabricated enormous offshore production modules there, including the 35,000-ton topsides for Shell’s Appomattox platform. The companies signed their initial shipbuilding partnership agreement at Kiewit’s Ingleside headquarters in July. For HD Hyundai, the attraction is clear. Kiewit brings established U.S. industrial capabilities, while Hyundai brings the vessel design expertise, production systems and shipyard management experience developed through decades of building ships at scale in South Korea. The companies intend to introduce HD Hyundai’s “Future of Shipyard” model, which incorporates digital twins, automated production systems, robotic welding and other advanced manufacturing technologies intended to improve productivity and reduce costs. That approach could be particularly important in the United States, where labor shortages, aging infrastructure and production inefficiencies have contributed to some of the world’s highest shipbuilding costs. The venture is initially targeting U.S. Navy auxiliary vessels, commercial ships and the fabrication of ship blocks and modules for other American shipbuilders. The latter could prove especially important. Supplying prefabricated sections to existing yards would allow the venture to contribute to U.S. shipbuilding programs without necessarily waiting for an entire vessel construction program of its own. The HD Hyundai–Kiewit project is the latest in a series of increasingly ambitious moves by South Korean shipbuilders to establish a permanent presence in the United States. Hanwha got an early start with its $100 million acquisition of Philly Shipyard in 2024, becoming the first major South Korean shipbuilder to take ownership of an American shipyard. In August 2025, Hanwha unveiled a $5 billion infrastructure plan aimed at transforming the Philadelphia facility into a high-volume production center. The plan includes additional docks, new quays, expanded block assembly capacity and advanced manufacturing technology. Hanwha has set an ambitious goal of increasing annual production from fewer than two vessels to as many as 20. The company has also begun building a commercial order pipeline, including plans for 10 Jones Act-compliant product tankers and LNG carriers, while pursuing opportunities in U.S. naval construction. HD Hyundai, meanwhile, has been building its own network of American partnerships. In July, it signed an agreement with Fraser Industries to explore shipyard modernization, including integrated design, production and management systems. Other South Korean shipbuilders are pursuing similar arrangements. Samsung Heavy Industries has established partnerships involving advanced shipbuilding technology, automated production and workforce training, while Hanwha Ocean has expanded its cooperation with U.S. defense and engineering companies. Those agreements gained additional momentum in July with the launch of the Korea–U.S. Shipbuilding Partnership Center in Washington, D.C. The center was established to coordinate investment, technology transfer, workforce development and industrial cooperation under the $150 billion MASGA initiative, which emerged from the broader U.S.–South Korea trade agreement reached in 2025. Its opening was accompanied by 15 agreements involving shipbuilders, technology companies, research institutions and other organizations from both countries. The proposed Hyundai–Kiewit yard offers one of the clearest examples yet of how that cooperation could translate into new industrial capacity. The investments are arriving at a time when the gap between American and Asian shipbuilding capacity remains enormous. According to new BIMCO analysis , Chinese shipyards now control 64% of the global shipbuilding order book, compared with 19% for South Korea and 6% for Japan. China also secured 74% of the compensated gross tonnage contracted worldwide over the past year, further strengthening its dominance across major commercial vessel sectors. The figures illustrate the scale of the challenge facing Washington as it attempts to restore domestic shipbuilding capacity after decades of decline. The United States is not starting from the same industrial position as its Asian competitors. South Korean and Chinese shipyards benefit from mature supplier networks, experienced workforces, established production systems and the economies of scale that come from building large numbers of ships. Rebuilding those capabilities in the United States will require more than new docks and modern equipment. An April report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that American Navy and Coast Guard shipbuilding programs have consistently suffered from cost overruns and delivery delays, with workforce shortages and infrastructure constraints among the major contributing factors. The report also warned that efforts to expand naval and commercial shipbuilding could increase competition for many of the same skilled workers and suppliers. That makes the involvement of established industrial contractors such as Kiewit particularly noteworthy. Unlike a traditional shipbuilder entering a new market, Kiewit already has an American workforce, complex fabrication experience and relationships across major industrial supply chains. Combined with HD Hyundai’s advanced production methods, those capabilities could offer a more practical starting point for expanding American shipbuilding than attempting to create an entirely new industrial operation from scratch. Still, significant questions remain about the proposed venture. HD Hyundai and Kiewit have not disclosed the project’s expected investment cost, identified the final shipyard location, announced construction contracts or provided production capacity targets. The proposed 2029 opening also leaves a relatively narrow window to develop a facility capable of undertaking complex commercial and naval construction. And while the companies have identified naval auxiliaries and commercial vessels as potential markets, neither has announced specific vessel orders for the new yard. That distinction matters. New shipbuilding capacity will only be sustainable if it is supported by a dependable pipeline of orders, a competitive cost structure and a workforce capable of maintaining production schedules. For Washington, the challenge is to ensure that the growing number of international partnerships becomes a durable American industrial base rather than a collection of high-profile investment announcements. For South Korea, the opportunity is substantial. American shipbuilding ambitions could create a long-term market for Korean technology, engineering expertise and industrial investment, while helping strengthen ties between two major maritime allies. The proposed HD Hyundai–Kiewit venture is another indication that the relationship is moving from government-level commitments toward concrete industrial projects. Whether those projects can deliver ships competitively, on schedule and at the scale Washington hopes to achieve will ultimately determine how much of America’s shipbuilding revival becomes reality. articles.title: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October
articles.summary: October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017."October…
articles.body: Strait of Hormuz Ship Attacks Reach New High in October Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Adobe Stock/S.Gvozd October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017. "October has seen the highest number of ship attacks on record," said Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Raydan, who maintains the institute's interactive shipping incident map, has recorded 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on February 28. The institute's map shows most of the attacks that took place in September and October were in the Strait of Hormuz. AROUND 3.5% OF WORLD SUPERTANKER FLEET ATTACKED The tally broadly aligns with data from the International Maritime Organization (IMO), which recorded a total of 120 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict with Iran began. The IMO lists more than 30 supertankers, or Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), that were damaged during the attacks, including 11 in October alone, a Reuters review of the IMO list and MarineTraffic vessel data showed. Each VLCC can carry about 2 million barrels of crude. The listed vessels account for about 3.5% of the total global VLCC fleet, which exceeds 900. More tankers came under attack as shipowners became increasingly willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf, lured by daily freight rates exceeding $1 million and steeper discounts offered by regional producers against dated Brent. "October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March," Greece-based consultancy Marisks said. Between October 5 and October 11, a dozen ships were attacked, marking also the highest weekly number of attacks since the conflict began, it also said. NOT ALL ATTACKS MAY BE CAPTURED IN DATA By intensifying attacks, Iran is seeking to slow the recovery in shipments and maintain pressure on global energy markets ahead of November's US midterm elections, Raydan said. Earlier this month, Reuters reported about Tehran adopting such tactics, citing two senior Iranian officials. UKMTO, the British maritime security service, which recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran conflict as of October 16, said it was struggling to capture the whole picture due to insufficient voluntary reporting by shippers. The UKMTO data also showed a sharp rise in ship damage caused by attacks in October. articles.title: First Russian Diesel From Putin-Trump Deal Heading for US
articles.summary: The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network By Igor Karasi / Shutterstock Oct 23 (Reuters) – The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday. Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US mid-term elections. Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices. The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulfur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022. Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere. “As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call. The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports. RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTS Since the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries. It also supplies Central Asia by rail. Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signaling trips to Turkey and Brazil. It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signaling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port-Said, LSEG data showed. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts. Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement. Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end. articles.body: U.S. Navy Secretary Visits Fincantieri Wisconsin Shipyards Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao visits Fincantieri shipyard in Wisconsin. Image courtesy Fincantieri Fincantieri hosted Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao and senior federal officials at its Marinette and Sturgeon Bay shipyards in Wisconsin, highlighting investments in advanced manufacturing, automation and expanded shipbuilding capacity as the company prepares for construction of the U.S. Navy's Landing Ship Medium (LSM) vessels . The delegation included Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Maritime Administration Administrator Stephen Carmel, OMB Associate Director for Shipbuilding Jerry Hendrix and Eugenio Santagata , General Manager of Fincantieri's Naval Vessels Division. George Moutafis, CEO of Fincantieri Marine Group, and Jan Allman, CEO of Fincantieri Marinette Marine, outlined the company's shipbuilding programs, capital investments and efforts to accelerate production. At Marinette, officials toured the automated panel production line and observed demonstrations of collaborative robots, augmented and virtual reality tools, and powered air-purifying respirators. Fincantieri is integrating these technologies to improve production efficiency and worker safety. At Sturgeon Bay, the delegation reviewed the shipyard's capabilities and its role in supporting simultaneous construction of multiple vessel classes. "This vital federal investment allows us to modernize" is not part of this release; instead, Moutafis emphasized the company's investments in workforce capabilities and advanced technologies to increase production rates and meet Navy requirements. The visit comes as Fincantieri Marinette Marine prepares to begin construction of four LSM vessels for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, subject to negotiations with program manager TOTE Services. In April, the Navy awarded Fincantieri an initial $30 million contract for procurement of critical materials associated with the LSM program. "Our Navy needs more skilled professionals like those I had the opportunity to meet today in order to remain the strongest Navy in the world," Cao said. The Wisconsin facilities are positioned to serve as the industrial center for Fincantieri's LSM work, expanding their role in the U.S. naval shipbuilding industrial base. articles.body: 18th Tug Delivered by Sanmar Shipyards to SAAM Towage Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 © Sanmar Shipyards Sanmar Shipyards has delivered SAAM XIMBAL, a new BOGAÇAY Class tug, to SAAM Towage, marking the 18th SANMAR-built tug delivered to the towage operator since 2018. Known as BOGAÇAY XCVI during construction in Türkiye, SAAM XIMBAL will operate from the Port of Lázaro Cárdenas on Mexico's Pacific coast, supporting demanding ship-handling operations at one of the country's major commercial ports. SAAM XIMBAL is based on the RAmparts 2400SX-MK|I design, developed exclusively for SANMAR by Canadian naval architects Robert Allan Ltd. The latest delivery brings the number of BOGAÇAY Class tugs in the SAAM Towage fleet to 13. Powered by two CAT 3516E main engines, each producing 2,350 KW at 1,800 rpm, SAAM XIMBAL combines high performance with environmentally responsible operation. A high level of onboard automation supports operational efficiency, while a sewage treatment unit and oily water separator further reduce the vessel's environmental impact as per SAAM sustainability requisites With an overall length of 24.4 meters, a molded beam of 12 meters, a least moulded depth of 4.5 meters and a navigational draught of 5.45 meters, SAAM XIMBAL combines compact dimensions with the power required for demanding harbor operations. The tug delivers over 80 tonnes of bollard pull and achieves a free-running speed of 13 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi 1 firefighting capability, further enhancing its operational versatility. SAAM XIMBAL joins a diverse group of SANMAR-built vessels already operating in the SAAM Towage fleet. Alongside the 13 BOGAÇAY Class tugs, these include three all-electric ElectRA harbor tugs and two powerful BIGAÇAY Class RAstar 29005X tugs.

articles.body: NOIA Launches Ocean Minerals Initiative Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 23, 2026 Courtesy NOIA The National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) has launched Ocean Minerals Forward, a new industry education and communications initiative examining the potential of deep-sea mineral resources to strengthen U.S. critical mineral supply chains, support domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. The initiative includes a dedicated website, a comprehensive report and educational resources covering seabed mineral development, offshore technologies, environmental considerations and the regulatory challenges facing the emerging industry. Critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper, manganese and rare earth elements are increasingly important to defense systems, advanced manufacturing, energy infrastructure and digital technologies. With global processing and refining capacity concentrated in a limited number of countries, NOIA argues that ocean mineral resources could complement terrestrial mining, recycling and imports from allied nations. “America cannot afford to remain dependent on foreign-controlled supply chains for the minerals that power our economy and national defense,” said NOIA President Erik Milito. “The ocean holds significant mineral resources, and companies across the U.S. and allied nations are bringing the technology, offshore expertise, and investment needed to unlock their potential.” A central theme of the initiative is the potential application of existing offshore oil and gas industry capabilities to seabed mineral exploration and recovery. Click here to download the full report. NOIA points to decades of experience in deepwater operations, including subsea robotics, autonomous underwater vehicles, geophysical surveying, dynamic positioning, specialized offshore vessels and environmental monitoring. These technologies could provide a foundation for future ocean mineral projects while creating opportunities for U.S. shipyards, ports, subsea contractors and equipment manufacturers. Environmental considerations are also addressed, including the potential effects of sediment plumes, impacts on deep-sea biodiversity and the need for environmental assessments, monitoring and regulatory oversight. The Ocean Minerals Forward report examines resource potential, global supply chain concentration, China's role in mineral processing, emerging collection technologies and opportunities for American offshore companies. NOIA said it plans to expand the platform with additional research, industry case studies and updates as technology, regulation and commercial opportunities develop. The initiative comes as the offshore industry evaluates the technical, environmental and economic feasibility of commercial seabed mineral recovery, an emerging sector where significant questions remain about environmental impacts, permitting and the development of viable processing and supply chains.

articles.title: Port of Riga to test resilient maritime communications under new partnership
articles.summary: The Port of Riga will serve as a testing site for secure maritime communication technologies under a new partnership between LVR Flote and HARDMODE. The two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory Forum in Riga on October 22, 2026. The agreement aims to develop and test...
articles.body: The Port of Riga will serve as a testing site for secure maritime communication technologies under a new partnership between LVR Flote and HARDMODE. The two companies signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) during the Techritory Forum in Riga on October 22, 2026. The agreement aims to develop and test communication systems that can support port operations during network disruptions and other challenging conditions. The partners will test new technologies in real port operations. They will also explore joint research projects and opportunities to introduce successful solutions at other European ports. Improving connectivity across port operations The project will focus on communication systems that remain operational when conventional networks become unavailable. HARDMODE develops solutions that combine several communication technologies. These include mobile, non-terrestrial, tactical and narrowband networks. The approach is designed to keep port equipment, sensors, vehicles, drones and personnel connected through different communication channels. It also uses a decentralized network structure, allowing connected devices to exchange information directly. Potential applications at the Port of Riga include infrastructure monitoring, hydrographic surveys, maintenance activities and navigation safety. The initiative comes amid concerns about GNSS interference in the Baltic Sea region, which has affected maritime activities in recent years. Partnership to support future port technologies LVR Flote provides technical services and supports infrastructure operations at the Port of Riga. Its involvement will allow the partners to assess new technologies against actual port requirements. “Port technical services have to keep running in everyday operations and in a crisis alike,” said Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote. The companies also plan to create an open testing framework for other technology providers. This could include developers of monitoring systems, sensors, automation solutions and digital port services. HARDMODE will contribute its communication technology, while LVR Flote will provide operational expertise and access to real-world testing conditions. The partnership also creates opportunities for joint research between Latvia and the Netherlands, reflecting HARDMODE’s connections to both countries. The companies intend to explore how successful pilot projects could eventually be deployed across other European ports. However, the announcement does not specify an investment value or a timetable for the planned trials.

Stock Photo: Nickeo23/Shutterstock By Weilun Soon Oct 23, 2026 (Bloomberg) –A little-known South Korean shipowner dominated oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz in September, data from intelligence firms suggest, with the group’s vessels moving more barrels than the next three owners combined. Ships owned by Sinokor Group carried 105.6 million barrels of crude through the waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with global markets, an analysis of ship-tracking and other data from intelligence firms Vortexa, Equasis and Signal Group showed. That’s equivalent to almost 40% of oil making the crossing last month. The next three players — the National Shipping Co. of Saudi Arabia, also known as Bahri, the Kuwait Oil Tanker Company, and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co.’s shipping unit — accounted for a combined 97.3 million barrels during the same period, according to Bloomberg calculations based on that data. The analysis considered ownership and not vessel operators. None of the four companies replied to requests for comment. Sinokor, owned by tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung, gained prominence from the early weeks of the Iran war, having amassed a huge tanker fleet in the run up to the conflict through purchases or time charters. When Hormuz was all but closed off, those tankers were snapped up at exorbitant rates by producers who needed to load oil or risk running out of storage space and then being forced to undertake costly shutdowns. Read more: Iran War Supercharges Secretive Korean Tycoon’s Big Tanker Bet As Gulf crude exports recover to close to pre-war levels, Sinokor is still among the most active owners in the so-called shuttling trade, with its vessels taking short trips to pick up oil from inside the Persian Gulf, sail through Hormuz and then discharge at ship-to-ship transfer points in the Gulf of Oman. Its tankers have assisted in the transporting of crude from Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and more recently also dabbled in Iraq and Qatar shipments, ship-tracking data show. The partners previously signed a carbon capture and storage (CCS) agreement in 2023 , as part of which they performed development studies and technical evaluations of potential storage areas offshore Peninsular Malaysia. articles.title: Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push
articles.summary: Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Operations Rio Tinto targets larger capesizes in $1.9bn Australian bauxite push Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 38 2 minutes read Bocimar Bocimar Mining giant Rio Tinto has approved a $1.9bn investment in a major bauxite expansion in Australia’s Queensland state, including an upgrade of its export facilities to accommodate larger capesize bulk carriers. The Kangwinan project on the western Cape York Peninsula will add 20m tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity, with first output targeted for 2029 and full production expected by 2032. The development will replace production from the ageing Andoom mine near Weipa, which is expected to reach the end of its life this decade, while also helping offset the planned closure of the Gove operation in the Northern Territory in 2029. Once fully operational, Kangwinan will lift annual capacity at Rio Tinto’s Weipa operations to around 44m tonnes, compared with current production of approximately 38m tonnes. The new mining centre will be located about 15 km southeast of Rio Tinto’s existing Amrun mine. A 15 km conveyor system will transport bauxite to expanded stockyards and the Amrun export wharf, which will be upgraded to handle larger capesize vessels. The mining group said the port expansion would improve shipping efficiency and reduce freight costs, strengthening its ability to supply overseas customers and Australian alumina refineries. Despite the larger vessels and additional mining capacity, analysts at SEB see limited upside for the capesize market from the investment. The bank noted that much of the new production will replace output from existing mines, leaving a relatively modest increase of around 6m tonnes compared with current Weipa production levels. Any additional volumes are also several years away. SEB further pointed out that shipments from Australia to China involve voyages roughly 3.3 times shorter than those from Guinea, where surging bauxite exports have been a major driver of capesize tonne-mile demand. The bank argued that additional Australian volumes could therefore work against the shift towards longer-haul Guinea-China trades, with the overall impact on dry bulk shipping likely to be negligible. Construction at Kangwinan is scheduled to accelerate in 2027, with the investment including $150m already approved for early works last year. The latest commitment follows Rio Tinto’s September agreement to acquire the neighbouring Aurukun bauxite project from Glencore and Mitsubishi, subject to regulatory approvals. The company intends to integrate the deposit into its longer-term development plans for the region, using existing and planned infrastructure. Bauxite’s growing importance to dry bulk shipping will be reflected at next April’s Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, with a standalone Bauxite Blitz session. Scheduled for April 28, the discussion will examine the expanding trade, shifting supply patterns and implications for future capesize demand. Confirmed speakers include Ernst Meyer, president and CEO of Torvald Klaveness, and Robert Haggquist, charterer and decarbonisation lead at South32. Braemar’s Derek Langston will moderate the session. articles.body: Business & Finance October 23, 2026 · 11 hours ago Eni, PTTEP forge JV to consolidate stakes in ADNOC’s giant offshore sour gas asset PTTEP and Eni have created Seela Energies to streamline operations and combine their stakes in an ADNOC-operated concession off the coast of the UAE. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Hail and Ghasha island under construction Source ADNOC As one of the world’s largest sour gas mega-projects continues to take shape in the waters of the Arabian Gulf, two energy heavyweights, Thailand’s PTT Exploration and Production Public Company (PTTEP) and Italy’s Eni, have pooled their stakes in Abu Dhabi’s massive Ghasha concession, carving out a newly minted joint venture (JV) called Seela Energies to unlock financing, share deep technical expertise, and scale up their activities for the long haul. PTTEP MENA, PTTEP’s wholly owned subsidiary, together with Eni Abu Dhabi, has established Seela Energies, with each company holding a 50% shareholding. Each of the founders holds a 10% participating interest in the Ghasha concession project , which will now be transferred to the newly formed JV. As a result, the duo will hold an indirect 10% interest in the project. According to PTTEP, all required regulatory, governmental, and partner approvals have been obtained, and all conditions precedent have been fulfilled. “The establishment of Seela Energies strengthens the collaboration between PTTEP and Eni, enhances access to financing, builds capability, shares expertise and supports potential future mutual growth in Middle East region, in line with PTTEP’s strategy to deliver long-term value through strategic partnerships,” emphasized the Thai player. Related Articles Fossil Energy WATCH: First steel cut for mega gas project set on zero-emission ops by entwining smart tech, carbon capture, hydrogen, nuclear, and renewable power 7 min read The Ghasha concession offshore Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, which is operated by the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC), is expected to produce more than 1.8 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day and 150,000 barrels of oil and condensate per day over the long term. This concession is considered to be one of the world's largest sulfur-rich gas development projects and a cornerstone of the UAE's strategy to achieve gas self-sufficiency and support rising international export demand. The development concept encompasses multiple fields, including Hail and Ghasha , located in shallow waters. This project utilizes a series of artificial islands rather than traditional platforms to drill and manage operations while minimizing environmental disturbance. Related Articles Fossil Energy First jacket comes to slide into place at huge offshore gas project 3 min read The Hail and Ghasha project, designed with an emphasis on low-emissions technology, aims to operate with net-zero carbon emissions by integrating carbon capture with a target of around 1.5 million tonnes of CO2 per year, low-carbon hydrogen use to replace fuel gas, and relying on less-emission-intensive power sources, such as nuclear and solar. ADNOC’s partners in the Ghasha concession, aside from Eni and PTTEP, which consolidated their joint stakes under Seela Energies, involved other companies across the broader project lifecycle, including Wintershall Dea, OMV, and Lukoil. The Ghasha development is envisioned to employ smart technology across all operations, allowing operators, technicians, and site personnel remote access to the project’s operations. Aside from a fully unmanned facility, ADNOC has set its sights on artificial intelligence (AI), such as predictive maintenance, for all critical rotating equipment. A few months ago, the operator, in partnership with Eni and PTTEP, put into place a structured financing transaction of up to $11 billion (AED 40.4 billion) for Hail and Ghasha sour gas development. The UAE giant’s financing model follows a series of midstream and infrastructure transactions, including a $4.9 billion (AED 18 billion) oil pipeline partnership and a $10.1 billion (AED 37.1 billion) gas pipeline agreement. It also comes after build-own-operate-transfer (BOOT) projects, such as the $3.8 billion (AED 14 billion) project to power and decarbonize offshore operations and the $2.2 billion (AED 8.3 billion) project to deliver sustainable water supplies to onshore operations. articles.title: Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data
articles.summary: Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to...
articles.body: Finance and Insurance Operations Fatigue, fear and the flaws in shipping’s safety data Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 202 1 minute read Britannia P&I Britannia P&I Seafarer fatigue, mental health and reluctance to report mistakes should become key considerations for marine insurers, banks and investors, according to new research warning that shipping is overlooking significant commercial risks hidden in its own data. The Sustainable Shipping Initiative’s (SSI) From Welfare to Risk report, published yesterday, examines 68 sources spanning accident investigations, insurance claims, academic studies and seafarer surveys. It finds consistent links between crew wellbeing and safety outcomes, particularly involving fatigue, mental health and psychological safety. Fatigue emerges as the most extensively documented risk factor. The report warns that understaffing and excessive workloads encourage the falsification of rest-hour records, concealing dangerous working conditions from compliance systems. Between a quarter and a third of seafarers do not feel safe raising concerns or reporting mistakes, potentially undermining the accuracy of incident and near-miss reporting. The findings reinforce earlier research covered by Splash . A World Maritime University study published in 2024 found 64.3% of surveyed seafarers adjusted their work/rest records. Another welfare review, reported by Splash last month, found just 49% of seafarers believed their most recent vessel carried sufficient crew to work safely without excessive fatigue. Insurance claims provide further evidence of the financial implications. Gard’s latest crew claims report identifies stress, fatigue and excessive workloads as important factors in onboard injuries, while illness accounts for almost 60% of crew claims. SSI argues insurers can already incorporate welfare indicators into loss-prevention programmes and underwriting discussions, while lenders could include them in borrower monitoring. However, the organisation cautions that current evidence remains insufficient to use welfare indicators as standalone predictors of future claims, insurance premiums or investment performance. The next challenge is connecting existing welfare surveys, accident investigations, port state control findings and insurance claims at vessel and operator level, allowing the industry to quantify how poor crew conditions translate into financial losses. The incident occurred when the ship deviated from its planned course because the second officer on watch fell asleep. articles.body: Containers Dry Cargo Europe Icon Energy faces shareholder revolt over dilution Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 108 1 minute read Icon Energy Icon Energy Nasdaq-listed Greek dry bulk owner Icon Energy is facing pressure from a significant shareholder to overhaul its capital structure and board, following accusations that repeated equity issuances have heavily diluted ordinary investors. Canada’s Hampton Financial, which holds 325,000 Icon shares representing approximately 9% of the company, has disclosed a letter sent to Icon’s management demanding changes to its preferred shares, dividend arrangements and corporate governance. Hampton, led by chairman and chief executive Peter Deeb, claims Icon has raised approximately $25m through common share issuances since its 2024 flotation, while ordinary shareholders have suffered substantial losses. The Canadian investment firm has also questioned the treatment of preferred shares held by Icon’s controlling shareholder and chief executive, Ismini Panagiotidi. Hampton is proposing that Icon exchange its outstanding Series A preferred shares for a new instrument with a $20m face value, a fixed 6% cash dividend and conversion rights priced at $5 per ordinary share. It also wants a one-for-one share dividend for existing ordinary shareholders and the appointment of a Hampton-nominated director. The investor argues that these measures would address dilution concerns while preserving Panagiotidi’s control of the business. The proposals have not been accepted or implemented, and the filing does not establish that legal proceedings have commenced. Icon, established in 2023, operates three bulk carriers. The company entered the Nasdaq market in July 2024 and subsequently expanded its fleet through secondhand acquisitions. Its most recent disclosed commercial moves include fixing the 63,668 dwt ultramax Charlie on an index-linked charter extending into 2027 and acquiring a minority investment in two containership projects. articles.body: Business & Finance October 23, 2026 · 13 hours ago Cheniere to fuel QatarEnergy with US Gulf Coast LNG through 2054 The multi-decade deal enables Cheniere to supply QatarEnergy with 4 million tonnes a year from its Gulf Coast facilities, starting in the early 2030s. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Corpus Christi LNG terminal operated by Cheniere Energy on the La Quinta Ship Channel in Corpus Christi, Texas, USA. Source: Bechtel In a move that reflects long-term energy planning, the U.S. Gulf Coast is locking in its commercial ties for the next three decades, as U.S.-headquartered energy player Cheniere has shown with a landmark liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal with Qatar’s state-owned oil and gas giant QatarEnergy, signing on to deliver millions of tonnes of LNG straight through 2054. Cheniere Energy’s subsidiaries, Sabine Pass Liquefaction (SPL) and Corpus Christi Liquefaction (CCL) , have each entered into long-term LNG sale and purchase agreements (SPAs) with QatarEnergy to supply a total of 4 million tonnes per annum (mtpa) of LNG through 2054. Jack Fusco , Cheniere’s Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer, commented: “These pivotal, multi-decade agreements with QatarEnergy, one of the world’s most important energy companies and a cornerstone of the global LNG industry, represent a major long-term commercial commitment and reinforce Cheniere’s position as the leader in U.S. LNG. “We take pride that Cheniere’s track record of operational excellence, reliability and long-term customer focus provided the foundation for this landmark commercial relationship with QatarEnergy. We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century.” While confirming the two SPAs for the purchase of LNG from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi facilities in Louisiana and Texas respectively, located along the United States Gulf Coast, QatarEnergy explained that these deals reflect its continued confidence in the long-term role of LNG in the global energy mix and its efforts to further develop a flexible, diversified, and globally competitive LNG portfolio. The SPAs were signed by Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi , Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs, President and CEO of QatarEnergy, and Jack Fusco , Chairman, President and CEO of Cheniere Energy. Minister Al-Kaabi said: “The signing of these two SPAs marks an important milestone in our LNG strategy. This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market. “The additional volumes will complement QatarEnergy’s existing LNG supplies, enhance our supply and trading portfolio, and strengthen our ability to serve customers across the globe.” The Qatari giant has agreed to purchase 2 mtpa of LNG from each of SPL and CCL on a free-on-board (FOB) basis for a purchase price indexed to the Henry Hub price plus a fixed fee. The deliveries under the SPAs will begin in the early 2030s and continue through the end of 2054, with 1 mtpa of the SPL SPA subject to a positive final investment decision (FID) for the first phase of the SPL Expansion project. Related Articles Clean Fuel Bechtel in charge of EPC scope for Cheniere’s LNG terminal expansion project 3 min read Cheniere Energy Partners is developing an expansion of the existing Sabine Pass liquefaction project with an expected total peak production capacity of up to approximately 20 mtpa of LNG, inclusive of estimated debottlenecking opportunities, which would grow the total production capacity of the SPL project to over 50 mtpa of LNG. The U.S. player expects to execute the SPL Expansion project in a phased approach, with the first phase anticipated to include a single train, Train 7, and a boil-off gas re-liquefaction unit, along with supporting infrastructure and tie-ins to the existing Sabine Pass LNG terminal. This phase has an expected total production capacity of over 6 mtpa of LNG, inclusive of estimated debottlenecking opportunities. In May 2026, the lump sum, turnkey engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract was penned with Bechtel Energy for the first phase of the SPL Expansion project, and the firm was given the go-ahead for early engineering and procurement under a limited notice to proceed (LNTP). Cheniere’s liquefaction portfolio consists of the Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi liquefaction facilities on the U.S. Gulf Coast, with total production capacity of approximately 56 mtpa of LNG in operation and an additional approximately 5 mtpa of expected production capacity under construction, inclusive of estimated debottlenecking opportunities. articles.title: Taylor Maritime agrees final owned bulker sale ahead of London exit
articles.summary: London-listed Taylor Maritime has agreed to sell its last owned bulk carrier for $15.1m, taking its fleet disposal programme to 56 vessels and putting total proceeds on course to reach almost $933m. The Ed Buttery-led company said the final sale is expected to complete in December, bringing to an end a three-year...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Greater China Taylor Maritime agrees final owned bulker sale ahead of London exit Adis Ajdin October 23, 2026 0 153 1 minute read London-listed Taylor Maritime has agreed to sell its last owned bulk carrier for $15.1m, taking its fleet disposal programme to 56 vessels and putting total proceeds on course to reach almost $933m. The Ed Buttery-led company said the final sale is expected to complete in December, bringing to an end a three-year selling campaign that has steadily dismantled one of the largest geared dry bulk fleets in the market. Since the beginning of 2023, Taylor Maritime has executed 55 vessel disposals with expected gross proceeds of $917.7m, at an average discount of 3.5% to fair market value. The latest agreement will lift the total to approximately $932.8m once completed. The move follows the completion of three handysize disposals announced earlier this month, which generated $48.6m. Those deals included transactions involving Buttery’s privately controlled T3 Holding vehicle, which acquired one vessel outright and a majority stake in a company holding another two handysizes alongside Hermes World Maritime. While the latest agreement covers Taylor Maritime’s last owned ship, one vessel remains on charter under a sale-and-leaseback arrangement with a purchase option. That contract expires in April 2027, and the company is assessing the most efficient way to exit the arrangement. Taylor Maritime expects to cease all commercial shipping operations by the end of 2026, with the wind-down now moving towards its final shareholder distributions. The company has confirmed a fourth compulsory capital return of $45m in November, taking the amount returned to investors since January to $263.4m. A further redemption is expected to be announced in December, subject to completion of the remaining vessel sale. The board then intends to put forward plans to cancel the company’s London listing. Taylor Maritime, which floated in May 2021, built its fleet to more than 50 vessels following the takeover of Grindrod Shipping before reversing course and embarking on an extensive asset disposal programme. The company formally adopted a managed realisation strategy in March this year, prioritising vessel sales and the return of capital to shareholders over continued fleet operations. articles.body: Americas Asia Shipyards HD Hyundai and Kiewit to build new US shipyard Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 0 182 1 minute read South Korea’s HD Hyundai has agreed to establish a joint venture with US engineering and construction giant Kiewit to build a new American shipyard, targeting operations from 2029. The venture, HD Kiewit Shipbuilding, plans to begin construction in 2027 at a yet-to-be-announced US industrial site. HD Hyundai expects the facility to create around 3,000 jobs once fully operational. The partners signed the agreement in Houston on Thursday, expanding a strategic shipbuilding partnership announced in July. The greenfield yard will incorporate HD Hyundai’s Future of Shipyard production model, including digital twins, automated manufacturing and robotic welding. It will target US Navy auxiliary vessels and commercial shipbuilding contracts, while also exploring the production of ship blocks and modules for other American yards. The move deepens HD Hyundai’s involvement in Washington’s efforts to revive domestic shipbuilding, supported by South Korea’s $150bn maritime investment commitment. The Korean group has been steadily expanding its American partnerships. In July, it signed an agreement with Fraser Industries to modernise Great Lakes shipyards, while August saw the launch of an automated welding pilot with Huntington Ingalls Industries at its Ingalls Shipbuilding facility in Mississippi. HD Hyundai has also partnered with Edison Chouest Offshore’s Tampa Ship to develop US-built LNG dual-fuel containerships, providing design, procurement and construction expertise. Its robotics division secured orders earlier this year to supply automated welding systems to Chouest yards in North America and Brazil. Unlike compatriot Hanwha’s acquisition of Philly Shipyard, HD Hyundai is pursuing newbuild yard development alongside upgrades to existing American facilities. articles.title: New index tracks how much the world cares about shipping
articles.summary: A new online index – much trailed on Splash – measuring how much attention the global shipping industry receives has gone live, offering maritime companies a way to assess public interest in shipping news and major incidents. Created by crisis communications specialist Dustin Eno, the Maritime Attention Index...
articles.body: Operations New index tracks how much the world cares about shipping Sam Chambers October 23, 2026 1 450 1 minute read Maxar Technologies Maxar Technologies A new online index – much trailed on Splash – measuring how much attention the global shipping industry receives has gone live, offering maritime companies a way to assess public interest in shipping news and major incidents. Created by crisis communications specialist Dustin Eno, the Maritime Attention Index combines Google searches, Wikipedia page views, social media activity and mainstream news coverage into a single daily score. “I built the index to answer a simple question with a single number: how much attention is shipping getting right now?” Eno explained. “Media monitoring tells you how much is being published about shipping, not how much attention it gets.” The publicly accessible platform allows users to examine historical attention spikes, compare incidents and identify how quickly public interest fades. Disasters such as the Ever Given, Wakashio and Dali casualties all show spikes. Eno’s analysis also reveals remarkably consistent patterns in how interest fades after major maritime incidents. When adjusted for duration and intensity, the attention curve surrounding this year’s Iran conflict closely resembles those generated by the Ever Given grounding and Baltimore bridge collapse. The index, which Eno has previously used in Splash commentary, is now available as an interactive public resource, accompanied by monthly analysis. Today’s reading stands at 69.3, with a score of 50 deemed normal. By way of comparison, in the opening fortnight of the US attacks on Iran in March this year, the index shot up to 332.3 points. The index goes back to the start of the 2020s, with its all-time high being the Ever Given’s closure of the Suez Canal in 2021. articles.summary: SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy SUNY Maritime College SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII is expected to return to its Fort Schuyler campus by mid-November after the federal government abruptly changed plans for a months-long deployment supporting the U.S. Navy. The reversal comes just weeks after the vessel departed New York for Norfolk, Virginia, where it was scheduled to undergo maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of a classified national security mission. In an October 21 message to the college community, SUNY Maritime President Rear Admiral John A. Okon confirmed the change. “I am pleased to share an important update on Empire State VII. The federal activation plan has changed, and the ship is now expected to return to Fort Schuyler for academic use, ship work, and with watches resuming no later than the middle of November,” Okon wrote. The announcement marks a significant shift from the original plans outlined by the U.S. Maritime Administration (MARAD), which ordered the vessel’s activation in August for an anticipated 170-day federal mission. An August 28 decision memorandum reviewed by gCaptain said the ship was needed to meet an urgent Military Sealift Command requirement and that no other suitable vessel was available within the required timeframe. Maritime Administrator Stephen Carmel described the activation as a “compelling strategic necessity.” The ship subsequently departed New York for Norfolk on September 30, with plans to remain there through October 30 for maintenance and flight deck certification ahead of follow-on operations supporting the Navy. The nature and destination of those operations were never publicly disclosed. It remains unclear what prompted the change in plans, whether the original military requirement has been withdrawn or reassigned, or how much of the planned work in Norfolk has been completed. For SUNY Maritime, however, the early return is welcome news. The vessel’s absence had threatened to disrupt academic programs, shipboard training and the sea time cadets need to qualify for U.S. Coast Guard licenses. “Empire State is more than a training ship. It is a classroom, a laboratory, and an essential part of the Maritime experience,” Okon said. Okon previously warned that losing the ship for much of the academic year would create significant challenges, and he pressed MARAD to return the vessel by February to keep the college’s 2027 Summer Sea Term on schedule. The revised timeline would bring the ship home roughly three months earlier than that requested deadline. Empire State VII , delivered in 2023, is the first of five purpose-built National Security Multi-Mission Vessels (NSMVs) developed by MARAD. The ships are designed primarily to train future merchant marine officers while also providing the federal government with additional sealift and emergency response capabilities. The vessel’s activation was expected to provide an early test of the NSMV program’s dual-use concept, demonstrating how a federally owned training ship could be called into service for national security missions. Instead, the shortened deployment raises questions about the circumstances behind the original urgent military requirement and the subsequent decision to release the vessel. “We will continue working with MARAD to confirm the exact details of the ship’s return and ensure we are ready to resume normal operations,” Okon said. articles.summary: China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new...

Join the leading maritime news network The 24,188 TEU capacity OOCL Spain pictured at the Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering (NACKS) shipyard in Nantong, China. Photo courtesy OOCL China has further cemented its dominance of global shipbuilding, capturing nearly three-quarters of new orders over the past year as the industry’s order book approaches record levels, according to new analysis from BIMCO. The global shipyard order book reached an estimated 203.2 million compensated gross tonnage (CGT) as of September 1, 2026, up 13% from 180 million CGT a year earlier. While slightly below the all-time high of 210.4 million CGT reached in May, the backlog remains above the previous record of 195.4 million CGT set in 2008. Chinese shipyards have been the biggest beneficiaries of the ordering boom, securing 74% of all CGT contracted over the past 12 months. China now controls 64% of the global order book, well ahead of South Korea at 19% and Japan at just 6%. China’s lead is even more pronounced across the major commercial shipping sectors. Its yards hold more than 72% of the order book in each of the six main vessel categories, including containerships, tankers, gas carriers, bulk carriers, other dry cargo ships and RoRo vessels. Together, those segments account for 88% of the global order book. Containerships are driving much of the growth. “Container ships dominate both the order book and its growth over the past 12 months. They account for 30% of CGT on order and 68% of the increase during the past year,” said Niels Rasmussen, BIMCO’s Chief Shipping Analyst. Chinese yards hold an especially commanding 81% share of the global containership order book. But the massive backlog also presents a growing challenge for shipbuilders, particularly in China, where scheduled deliveries are set to far exceed recent production levels. Based on each country’s highest annual output between 2021 and 2025, Chinese shipyards have enough orders to keep them busy for an average of 4.2 years. That compares with just 1.9 years for South Korean yards and 1.7 years for Japanese yards. The challenge is the sheer volume of ships scheduled for delivery. Combined output from China, South Korea and Japan reached 40.1 million CGT in 2025, but scheduled deliveries climb to 55.9 million CGT in 2027 and 60 million CGT in 2028. China faces the steepest increase, with its shipyards scheduled to deliver a record 44 million CGT in 2028, nearly double the 22.7 million CGT delivered in 2025. Meeting those commitments will require a significant increase in production capacity. BIMCO estimates that if capacity is instead measured against the highest annual output delivered or scheduled between 2021 and 2030, China’s order book coverage falls to 2.1 years, compared with 1.6 years for both South Korea and Japan. The figures highlight a potential downside to China’s rapid shipbuilding expansion. While its yards currently enjoy an enormous backlog, the investments needed to meet delivery commitments could leave the industry with excess capacity if demand for new ships slows. “China has further strengthened its position as the world’s leading shipbuilding nation, but its shipyards must raise annual output to new record highs in order to deliver,” Rasmussen said. “The capacity expansion needed to achieve this could increase the risk of underutilisation if contracting weakens in the future.” Sign up for gCaptain’s newsletter and never miss an update Essential maritime and offshore news, insights, and updates delivered daily straight to your inbox Dive into a sea of curated content with our weekly ‘Dispatch’ email.
